concepts: Maxima of a function and comparison of exponentials
questions.question: If the function $f(x)=\left(\frac1x\right)^{2x}$, $x>0$ attains the maximum value at $x=\frac1e$, then :
questions.key_idea: Since $x=\frac1e$ is the maximum, $f\left(\frac1e\right)>f\left(\frac1\pi\right)$ turns into $e^{\pi}>\pi^{e}$.
solution: $f(x)=\left(\frac1x\right)^{2x}$, so $\ln f=-2x\ln x$ and $\frac{f'}{f}=-2(\ln x+1)$; $f'=0$ at $x=\frac1e$, where $f'$ changes from $+$ to $-$: the maximum, as given.
The maximum is the greatest value, and $\frac1\pi\neq\frac1e$, so $f\left(\frac1e\right)>f\left(\frac1\pi\right)$.
Take the positive square root: $e^{1/e}>\pi^{1/\pi}$. Raise both sides to the power $e\pi>0$: $e^{\pi}>\pi^{e}$.
Check of the others: $e^{2\pi}\approx535>(2\pi)^e\approx148$, so (A) is false and hence (C) is false; $(2e)^\pi\approx204<\pi^{2e}\approx504$, so (D) is false.

alternate_solutions.idea: Tangent-line inequality $e^t\ge et$ at $t=\frac\pi e$ gives $e^{\pi/e}>\pi$ directly.
solution: $h(t)=e^t$ is convex, so it lies above its tangent at $t=1$: $e^t\ge e\,t$ for all $t$, with equality only at $t=1$.
Raise both sides to the power $e>0$: $e^{\pi}>\pi^{e}$.
So (B) holds. Numerically $e^\pi\approx23.14>\pi^e\approx22.46$ (and (A), (D) are false by size, as before). Same answer.

useful_results: For $x>0$, $x\neq e$: $e^x>x^e$ (from $e^t\ge et$ with $t=\frac xe$). So $e^\pi>\pi^e$ and, for any $a>0$, $e^a\ge ea$.
$\frac{\ln x}{x}$ increases on $(0,e)$ and decreases on $(e,\infty)$ with maximum at $x=e$; hence for $a,b\ge e$ with $a<b$: $a^b>b^a$.
$x^{1/x}$ has its maximum at $x=e$ and $\left(\frac1x\right)^{x}$ at $x=\frac1e$ - take logarithms and set the derivative to $0$.
Comparing $a^b$ with $b^a$: compare $\frac{\ln a}{a}$ with $\frac{\ln b}{b}$.

concepts: Local maxima and minima by the first derivative test
questions.question: Let $f(x)=4\cos^3x+3\sqrt3\cos^2x-10$. The number of points of local maxima of $f$ in the interval $(0,2\pi)$ is :
questions.key_idea: Factor $f'(x)=-6\sin x\cos x\,(2\cos x+\sqrt3)$ and read the sign changes on $(0,2\pi)$.
solution: Zeros of $f'$ in $(0,2\pi)$: $\sin x=0$ at $\pi$; $\cos x=0$ at $\frac\pi2,\frac{3\pi}2$; $\cos x=-\frac{\sqrt3}2$ at $\frac{5\pi}6,\frac{7\pi}6$.

Signs of $f'$ on the intervals $\left(0,\frac\pi2\right),\left(\frac\pi2,\frac{5\pi}6\right),\left(\frac{5\pi}6,\pi\right),\left(\pi,\frac{7\pi}6\right),\left(\frac{7\pi}6,\frac{3\pi}2\right),\left(\frac{3\pi}2,2\pi\right)$ are $-,+,-,+,-,+$.
$f'$ changes from $+$ to $-$ at $\frac{5\pi}6$ and at $\frac{7\pi}6$ only: local maxima there.
So the number of points of local maxima is $2$: option (C).

alternate_solutions.idea: Write $f=g(c)$ with $c=\cos x$; maxima of $g$ at interior values of $c$ pull back to the points of $x$.
solution: $g''\left(-\frac{\sqrt3}2\right)=-6\sqrt3<0$: $g$ has a local maximum at $c=-\frac{\sqrt3}2$; $g''(0)=6\sqrt3>0$: a local minimum at $c=0$.
Where $\sin x\neq0$, $c=\cos x$ is strictly monotonic in $x$ locally, so local maxima/minima of $f$ in $x$ correspond to those of $g$ in $c$.
$\cos x=-\frac{\sqrt3}2$ has two roots in $(0,2\pi)$: $\frac{5\pi}6$ and $\frac{7\pi}6$, both local maxima; $\cos x=0$ gives minima.
At $x=\pi$ ($c=-1$, where $\sin x=0$): $g'(-1)=6(-1)(\sqrt3-2)>0$, so $f$ has a local minimum there, since $\cos x\ge-1$ rises on both sides.
Hence exactly $2$ local maxima: option (C). Same answer.

useful_results: For $f(x)=g(\cos x)$ or $g(\sin x)$: $f'=-g'(\cos x)\sin x$, so critical points come from $g'(c)=0$ and from $\sin x=0$ (the ends $c=\pm1$ of the range).
At an interior critical value $c_0$ of $g$ a local max of $g$ gives a local max of $f$ at every $x$ with $\cos x=c_0$.
Near $x=\pi$, $\cos x\approx-1+\frac{(x-\pi)^2}2$, so $f$ has a local minimum there iff $g'(-1)>0$ (and near $x=0$ or $2\pi$, a local minimum iff $g'(1)<0$).
Sign table on $(0,2\pi)$ alternates only across factors with odd multiplicity.

concepts: Local maxima and minima of a cubic
Quadratic equation with given roots
questions.question: If the function $f(x)=2x^3-9ax^2+12a^2x+1$, $a>0$ has a local maximum at $x=\alpha$ and a local minimum at $x=\alpha^2$, then $\alpha$ and $\alpha^2$ are the roots of the equation :
questions.key_idea: The critical points are $a$ and $2a$, and the maximum comes first, so $\alpha=a$ and $\alpha^2=2a$.
solution: $f'(x)=0$ gives $x=a,\,2a$. As $a>0$, the leading coefficient is positive, so the local maximum is at the smaller value $a$ and the local minimum at $2a$.
The roots $2$ and $4$ have sum $6$ and product $8$: the equation is $x^2-6x+8=0$, option (C).
questions.correction_note: PDF writes the factor as (x^2 - 3a + 2a^2); the middle term must be 3ax: f'(x) = 6(x^2 - 3ax + 2a^2). The factorisation (x-a)(x-2a) and the answer (C) are right.

alternate_solutions.idea: The two critical points are $a$ apart, so $\alpha^2-\alpha=a=\alpha$ at once.
solution: $f'(x)=6(x-a)(x-2a)$: critical points $a$ and $2a$, with the maximum at the smaller one.
Their gap is $2a-a=a$, while the given points are $\alpha$ and $\alpha^2$, whose gap is $\alpha^2-\alpha$ (positive, as min is to the right of max).
Also the maximum point is $\alpha=a$ itself, so $\alpha^2-\alpha=a=\alpha$, i.e. $\alpha^2=2\alpha$ and $\alpha=2$ (as $\alpha=a>0$).
The required equation has sum of roots $\alpha+\alpha^2=6$ and product $\alpha^3=8$: $x^2-6x+8=0$. Same answer (C).

useful_results: For a cubic with positive leading coefficient, the local maximum is at the smaller root of $f'$ and the local minimum at the larger; reverse for a negative leading coefficient.
$f(x)=2x^3-3(p+q)x^2+6pqx+c$ has $f'=6(x-p)(x-q)$: critical points are exactly $p$ and $q$; here $p=a$, $q=2a$.
A quadratic with roots $r,s$ is $x^2-(r+s)x+rs=0$; here $\alpha+\alpha^2=6$, $\alpha\cdot\alpha^2=\alpha^3=8$.
Always reject solutions that violate the stated sign condition ($a>0$ removes $\alpha=0$).

concepts: Maxima and minima in word problems (arithmetic progression)
questions.question: In an A.P., the sixth term $a_6=2$. If the product $a_1a_4a_5$ is the greatest, then the common difference of the A.P. is equal to :
questions.key_idea: Use $a_6=2$ to write $a_1,a_4,a_5$ in terms of $d$, then maximise the cubic $P(d)$.
solution: Let the first term be $a$ and the common difference $d$. Given $a+5d=2$ ... (1).

$\frac{dP}{dd}$ is negative for $d<\frac23$, positive for $\frac23<d<\frac85$ and negative for $d>\frac85$, so $P$ has its local maximum at $d=\frac85$ ($P=\frac{72}{25}$) and a local minimum at $d=\frac23$.
questions.correction_note: PDF writes the product as a1 a5 a6 = a(a+4d)(a+3d); the product in the question is a1 a4 a5 = a(a+3d)(a+4d) (the expression used afterwards is right). Also, P(d) = -10d^3 + ... tends to +infinity as d -> -infinity, so P has no global maximum; the question means the local maximum d = 8/5. Key (B) kept.
useful_results: In an A.P. with $a_n$ given, write every term as $a_n+(k-n)d$ and reduce to a single variable $d$.
A cubic with negative leading coefficient has its local maximum at the larger root of $P'$ (and its local minimum at the smaller).
Beware 'greatest' for an unbounded cubic: the maximum is local unless $d$ is restricted (e.g. positive terms). Here $P(8/5)=72/25$.
Product of three terms with two moving factors: use $\frac{P'}{P}=\sum\frac{c_i}{x_i}$ when the factors are linear.

concepts: Local maxima and minima at a cusp and at a stationary point
questions.question: The function $f(x)=2x+3\,x^{2/3}$, $x\in\mathbb{R}$, has :
options: exactly one point of local minima and no point of local maxima
exactly two points of local maxima and exactly one point of local minima
exactly one point of local maxima and exactly one point of local minima
exactly one point of local maxima and no point of local minima
questions.answer: (C) exactly one point of local maxima and exactly one point of local minima
questions.key_idea: $f'$ vanishes at $x=-1$ and does not exist at $x=0$ (a cusp): check the sign change at both.
solution: $f'(x)=0$ at $x=-1$, and $f'$ does not exist at $x=0$ (while $f$ is continuous there).
For $x<-1$: numerator $<0$, denominator $<0$, so $f'>0$. For $-1<x<0$: numerator $>0$, denominator $<0$, so $f'<0$. For $x>0$: $f'>0$. Signs: $+,\,-,\,+$.
So the maximum (M) is at $x=-1$ and the minimum (m) at $x=0$.
Exactly one local maximum and exactly one local minimum: option (C).

alternate_solutions.idea: Substitute $t=x^{1/3}$ (an increasing bijection of $\mathbb{R}$): the cusp becomes an ordinary cubic.
solution: $t=x^{1/3}$ is strictly increasing and one-one on $\mathbb{R}$, so local maxima/minima of $f$ in $x$ are those of $F(t)=2t^3+3t^2$ in $t$.
$F'$ is $+$ for $t<-1$, $-$ for $-1<t<0$, $+$ for $t>0$ (a cubic with positive leading coefficient).
So $F$ has a local maximum at $t=-1$ (i.e. $x=-1$) and a local minimum at $t=0$ (i.e. $x=0$).
One local maximum and one local minimum: option (C). Same answer.

useful_results: $x^{p/q}$ terms give points where $f'$ does not exist; these must be tested as candidates (cusp / vertical tangent) along with $f'=0$.
Substituting $t=x^{1/q}$ (odd $q$, increasing and one-one) turns $f$ into a polynomial and preserves local extrema.
For $x^{2/3}$ the graph has a cusp pointing down at the origin: $x^{2/3}\ge0$ gives a local minimum at $0$ for $f=x^{2/3}$ alone.
A point where $f'$ is undefined is an extremum only if $f$ is continuous there and $f'$ changes sign.

concepts: Maximum area of a triangle (optimisation)
questions.question: The maximum area of a triangle whose one vertex is at $(0,0)$ and the other two vertices lie on the curve $y=-2x^2+54$ at points $(x,y)$ and $(-x,y)$, where $y>0$, is :
questions.key_idea: Base $2x$ and height $y=54-2x^2$ give the area as a cubic in $x$.
solution: The vertices are $(0,0)$, $(x,y)$ and $(-x,y)$: base $=2x$ (the chord $y=\text{const}$), height $=y=54-2x^2$.
$\frac{dA}{dx}=0\Rightarrow x=\pm3$; with $x>0$ take $x=3$ ($\frac{d^2A}{dx^2}=-12x<0$, a maximum; also $A=0$ at $x=0$ and $x=3\sqrt3$).

alternate_solutions.idea: AM-GM on $4x^2,\ 54-2x^2,\ 54-2x^2$, whose sum is the constant $108$.
solution: Write $A^2=\frac14\cdot\left(4x^2\right)\left(54-2x^2\right)\left(54-2x^2\right)$; the three factors are positive with constant sum $4x^2+2(54-2x^2)=108$.
Equality when $4x^2=54-2x^2$, i.e. $x^2=9$, $x=3$ - attainable. Maximum area $108$: option (D). Same answer.

useful_results: Triangle with a vertex at the origin and the other two at $(\pm x,y)$: area $=xy$.
Maximise $x^p(c-qx^2)^r$-type products without calculus by AM-GM: split into pieces whose sum is constant.
For $A=ax-bx^3$ the maximum is at $x=\sqrt{\frac{a}{3b}}$ with value $\frac{2a}{3}\sqrt{\frac a{3b}}$; here $a=54,b=2$: $x=3$, $A=108$.
Check the endpoints of the admissible domain ($y>0$ means $0<x<3\sqrt3$) - both give zero area.

concepts: Absolute maximum and minimum on a closed interval
questions.question: Let $f(x)=(x+3)^2(x-2)^3$, $x\in[-4,4]$. If $M$ and $m$ are the maximum and minimum values of $f$, respectively in $[-4,4]$, then the value of $M-m$ is :
questions.key_idea: Absolute extrema on $[-4,4]$ are among the endpoints and the critical points $-3,-1,2$.

alternate_solutions.idea: No derivative: bound $f$ piece by piece, using AM-GM for the dip between $-3$ and $2$.
solution: On $[2,4]$ both $(x+3)^2$ and $(x-2)^3$ are non-negative and increasing, so $0\le f\le f(4)=392$. On $[-4,2]$, $f\le0$. Hence $M=392$.
On $[-3,2]$ apply AM-GM to the five non-negative numbers $\frac{x+3}2,\frac{x+3}2,\frac{2-x}3,\frac{2-x}3,\frac{2-x}3$ whose sum is $5$.

useful_results: Absolute extrema of a continuous function on $[a,b]$: compare $f$ at the endpoints and at all critical points (including where $f'$ does not exist).
For $f=(x-a)^p(x-b)^q$: $f'=(x-a)^{p-1}(x-b)^{q-1}\left[p(x-b)+q(x-a)\right]$; the extra critical point is $x=\frac{pb+qa}{p+q}$, here $\frac{2\cdot2+3(-3)}{5}=-1$.
AM-GM with weights: $(x-a)^p(b-x)^q\le p^pq^q\left(\frac{b-a}{p+q}\right)^{p+q}$ on $[a,b]$, with equality at $x=\frac{pb+qa}{p+q}$.
The factor $(x-2)^2$ in $f'$ has even power, so $x=2$ is a stationary point of inflection, not an extremum; $x=-3$ is a local maximum and $x=-1$ a local minimum.

concepts: Maximum of a function on a closed interval
Multiple-angle trigonometric identities
questions.question: $\max_{0\le x\le\pi}\left\{x-2\sin x\cos x+\frac13\sin3x\right\}=$
questions.key_idea: $f'=(\cos x-1)(4\cos^2x-3)$ has simple roots $\frac\pi6,\frac{5\pi}6$; compare the maximum with the endpoint $f(\pi)$.
solution: $f'(x)=1-2\cos2x+\cos3x=0$. With $c=\cos x$ this is $(c-1)(4c^2-3)=0$, so in $(0,\pi)$: $x=\frac{5\pi}6,\ \frac\pi6$.
$f''\left(\frac{5\pi}6\right)=4\sin\frac{5\pi}3-3\sin\frac{5\pi}2=-2\sqrt3-3<0$, so $x=\frac{5\pi}6$ is a point of maxima.
The interval is closed, so compare with the endpoints: $f(0)=0$ and $f(\pi)=\pi\approx3.14<3.82$ (and $x=\frac\pi6$ is a local minimum).
useful_results: $1-2\cos2x+\cos3x=(\cos x-1)(4\cos^2x-3)$: use $\cos2x=2c^2-1$, $\cos3x=4c^3-3c$ to factor trigonometric derivatives.
For $F(x)=x-\sin2x+\frac13\sin3x$ the derivative $\ge0$ exactly where $4\cos^2x\le3$ on $(0,\pi)$, i.e. between $\frac\pi6$ and $\frac{5\pi}6$.
On a closed interval always compare local extremum values with the endpoint values; here the endpoint value $\pi$ is less than the local maximum $3.82$.
Double and triple-angle formulas: $\sin2x=2\sin x\cos x$, $\sin3x=3\sin x-4\sin^3x$, $\cos3x=4\cos^3x-3\cos x$.

concepts: Condition for local maximum and minimum of a cubic (roots of the derivative)
questions.question: Let the function $f(x)=2x^3+(2p-7)x^2+3(2p-9)x-6$ have a maxima for some value of $x<0$ and a minima for some value of $x>0$. Then, the set of all values of $p$ is
questions.key_idea: A cubic with positive leading coefficient has its maximum at the smaller root of $f'$ and its minimum at the larger, so $f'$ must have roots of opposite signs.
solution: Its smaller root gives the maximum and its larger root the minimum, so we need the smaller root $<0<$ the larger root.
For an upward parabola this happens exactly when $f'(0)<0$.

alternate_solutions.idea: Vieta: the roots of $f'$ have opposite signs iff their product is negative.
solution: The maximum is at $x_1$ and the minimum at $x_2$ (positive leading coefficient), so we need $x_1<0<x_2$, i.e. $x_1x_2<0$.
$x_1x_2<0\Rightarrow\frac{2p-9}2<0\Rightarrow p<\frac92$; a negative product also forces real distinct roots, so no discriminant condition is needed.

useful_results: A quadratic with positive leading coefficient has roots of opposite signs iff $f'(0)<0$ (equivalently product of roots $<0$): this alone guarantees real distinct roots.
If the maximum is required at $x<0$ and the minimum at $x>0$ for $ax^3+\dots$ with $a>0$, the condition is $\frac{c}{3a}<0$ where $c$ is the coefficient of $x$.
Reverse the roles for a negative leading coefficient (then the maximum is at the larger root).
Other positional conditions on roots of $f'$: both roots positive iff sum $>0$, product $>0$, discriminant $>0$.

concepts: Common extreme point and common root of derivatives
questions.question: If the functions $f(x)=\frac{x^3}3+2bx+\frac{ax^2}2$ and $g(x)=\frac{x^3}3+ax+bx^2$, $a\neq2b$ have a common extreme point, then $a+2b+7$ is equal to :
questions.key_idea: A common extreme point is a common root of $f'$ and $g'$; subtracting forces that root to be $x=1$.
solution: A common extreme point is a common root of $f'(x)=0$ and $g'(x)=0$; subtract: $(2b-a)-x(2b-a)=0$.
$(2b-a)(1-x)=0$ and $a\neq2b$, so $x=1$ is the common root.

alternate_solutions.idea: The two derivatives are mirror images ($a\leftrightarrow2b$), so $x=1$ is special at once.
solution: At $x=1$: $f'(1)=1+a+2b=g'(1)$ for every $a,b$, so $1$ is a root of one iff it is a root of both.
Any other common root $r$ would satisfy $f'(r)-g'(r)=(a-2b)(r-1)=0$, impossible for $a\neq2b$ unless $r=1$.
So the common root is $x=1$ and $1+a+2b=0$, giving $a+2b+7=6$: option (C). Same answer.

useful_results: Two polynomials $x^2+ax+c$ and $x^2+cx+a$ always share the root $x=1$ iff $1+a+c=0$; the difference of the two equations is $(a-c)(x-1)$.
A common root of $P(x)=0$ and $Q(x)=0$ also satisfies $P(x)-Q(x)=0$: subtract to lower the degree.
An extreme point needs $f'=0$ and a sign change; with roots $1$ and $2b$ (for $f'$) and $1$ and $a$ (for $g'$) this needs $2b\neq1$ and $a\neq1$.
Here Vieta gives the other roots as $2b$ and $a$ from the products of roots.

concepts: Bounds on derivatives and comparison of functions
Monotonicity of increasing functions
questions.question: Let $f(x)=2x+\tan^{-1}x$ and $g(x)=\log_e\left(\sqrt{1+x^2}+x\right)$, $x\in[0,3]$. Then :
options: there exists $\hat x\in[0,3]$ such that $f'(\hat x)<g'(\hat x)$
questions.key_idea: Bound $f'$ and $g'$ on $[0,3]$; both functions are increasing, so each maximum is at $x=3$.
solution: Hence $2+\frac1{10}\le f'(x)\le3$, i.e. $\frac{21}{10}\le f'(x)\le3$, and $\frac1{\sqrt{10}}\le g'(x)\le1$.
(A): $\min f'=\frac{21}{10}$ but $1+\max g'=2$, so (A) is false.
(C): $f'(x)\ge\frac{21}{10}>1\ge g'(x)$ for all $x$ in $[0,3]$, so no $\hat x$ has $f'(\hat x)<g'(\hat x)$: (C) is false.
$f'$ and $g'$ are both positive, so $f$ and $g$ are increasing: $\max f=f(3)=6+\tan^{-1}3\approx7.25$.
questions.correction_note: PDF's option numbering is inconsistent: after bounding f' and g' it says 'option (4) is incorrect' (it means (C); (D) is the correct option), and it never discusses (B). Corrected so that (A), (B), (C) are shown false and (D) true; answer D unchanged.

alternate_solutions.idea: Study $h=f-g$: $h(0)=0$ and $h'>0$, so $f>g$ throughout and no logarithm values are needed.
solution: So $h$ is increasing and $h(x)>0$ for $x\in(0,3]$: $f>g$ there, so no interval $(x_1,x_2)\subset(0,3)$ has $f<g$ - (B) is false.
(A): $\min f'=f'(3)=\frac{21}{10}$ and $\max g'=g'(0)=1$, so $\min f'\neq1+\max g'=2$ - false.
(D): both functions are increasing, so $\max f=f(3)>g(3)=\max g$ because $h(3)>0$. Hence (D). Same answer.

useful_results: To compare $\max f$ and $\max g$ of increasing functions, compare $f(b)$ and $g(b)$ - or study $h=f-g$ and its sign.
$\ln\left(x+\sqrt{1+x^2}\right)=\sinh^{-1}x$ has derivative $\frac1{\sqrt{1+x^2}}$, $\int\frac{dx}{\sqrt{1+x^2}}=\ln\left(x+\sqrt{1+x^2}\right)$.
If $f(a)=g(a)$ and $f'>g'$ on $(a,b]$, then $f>g$ on $(a,b]$ (the Mean Value Theorem argument for $h=f-g$).
Bounds on $\frac1{1+x^2}$ over $[0,3]$ come from the monotone decrease: it ranges from $1$ down to $\frac1{10}$.

concepts: Absolute maximum and minimum of a modulus function
questions.question: The sum of the absolute maximum and minimum values of the function $f(x)=|x^2-5x+6|-3x+2$ in the interval $[-1,3]$ is equal to :
questions.key_idea: Remove the modulus using the sign of $(x-2)(x-3)$ and show $f$ is decreasing on $[-1,3]$, so the extremes are at the ends.
solution: $f'(x)=2x-8$ on $[-1,2]$ and $f'(x)=-2x+2$ on $[2,3]$; both are negative, so $f$ is decreasing on $[-1,3]$ (the pieces meet at $f(2)=-4$).
questions.correction_note: PDF writes 'f(2) = 4 - 16 + 8 = -4 = 4' (the value is -4, not 4) and labels its sketch 'max = 17, min = -17'; the correct values are f(2) = -4, max = 17, min = -7. Final answer 10 unchanged. The decreasing argument was added.

alternate_solutions.idea: Complete the square on each piece: both vertices lie outside their pieces on the right side, so $f$ decreases throughout.
solution: On $[-1,2]$: $f=x^2-8x+8=(x-4)^2-8$, a parabola with vertex at $x=4$, to the right of $2$, so it is decreasing on $[-1,2]$.
On $[2,3]$: $f=-x^2+2x-4=-(x-1)^2-3$, vertex at $x=1$, to the left of $2$, so it is decreasing on $[2,3]$.
Both pieces equal $-4$ at $x=2$, so $f$ is continuous and decreasing on $[-1,3]$.
Hence the maximum is $f(-1)=(-5)^2-8=17$ and the minimum is $f(3)=-4-3=-7$.

useful_results: For $|q(x)|+\text{linear}$ on an interval, split at the roots of $q$ and write each piece as a quadratic; the absolute extrema occur at endpoints, roots of $q$ (kinks) or the vertices lying in the pieces.
A piecewise function that is decreasing on every piece and continuous is decreasing: its extremes are at the two ends.
At the kinks $x=2,3$ (roots of $x^2-5x+6$), $f$ may be non-differentiable; test them as candidates, here $f(2)=-4$ is neither extreme.
Vertex of $x^2+bx+c$ is at $x=-\frac b2$; compare with the piece's interval before using the vertex.

concepts: Number of real roots of a cubic by its local extreme values
questions.question: If the set of all values of $a$, for which the equation $5x^3-15x-a=0$ has three distinct real roots, is the interval $(\alpha,\beta)$, then $\beta-2\alpha$ is equal to ___________.
questions.key_idea: A cubic has three distinct real roots iff its local maximum and minimum values have opposite signs.
solution: Three distinct real roots need the local maximum $f(-1)=10-a$ and local minimum $f(1)=-10-a$ to have opposite signs: $f(1)f(-1)<0$.

alternate_solutions.idea: Use the discriminant: $x^3+px+q=0$ has three distinct real roots iff $4p^3+27q^2<0$.
solution: Divide by $5$: $x^3-3x-\frac a5=0$, with $p=-3$ and $q=-\frac a5$.

useful_results: For $ax^3+bx^2+cx+d=0$ with $f'$ having real roots $x_1<x_2$: three distinct real roots iff $f(x_1)\cdot f(x_2)<0$; a repeated root iff the product is $0$; one real root iff $>0$.
Equivalent graphical view: $a=5x^3-15x$ is cut by the horizontal line at height $a$ in three points iff $a$ lies strictly between local min value $-10$ and local max value $10$.
Depressed cubic $x^3+px+q$: discriminant $-4p^3-27q^2$; three distinct real roots iff it is positive.
The interval for $a$ here is symmetric because $5x^3-15x$ is an odd function.

concepts: Maximum area of an inscribed rectangle (optimisation)
questions.question: Let $A$ be the region enclosed by the parabola $y^2=2x$ and the line $x=24$. Then the maximum area of the rectangle inscribed in the region $A$ is ___________.
questions.key_idea: Take the rectangle symmetric about the axis with corners $(x,\pm y)$ on the parabola and the far side on $x=24$.
solution: Take the rectangle with vertices $(x,\pm y)$ on the parabola $y^2=2x$ and its other two vertices on the line $x=24$.

alternate_solutions.idea: AM-GM on $2y^2,\ 48-y^2,\ 48-y^2$, whose sum is the constant $96$.
solution: The three factors are positive with constant sum $2y^2+2(48-y^2)=96$; AM-GM gives product $\le32^3$.
Equality when $2y^2=48-y^2$, i.e. $y=4$ - attainable. Maximum area $128$. Same answer.

useful_results: Rectangle inscribed in the region $y^2=4ax$, $x\le h$: with corners $(x,\pm y)$ the area is $2y(h-x)$; maximum at $x=\frac h3$, i.e. $y^2=\frac{4ah}{3}$.
Here $h=24$ and $y^2=2x$: $x=\frac{24}3=8$, $y=4$ and the area is $2\cdot4\cdot16=128$.
Make the single variable the one that removes the square root ($y$ rather than $x$).
At $x\to0$ and $x\to24$ the area tends to $0$, so the stationary point is the maximum.

concepts: Local minimum of a cubic
Rational inequality
questions.question: Let the set of all positive values of $\lambda$, for which the point of local minimum of the function $\left(1+x(\lambda^2-x^2)\right)$ satisfies $\frac{x^2+x+2}{x^2+5x+6}<0$, be $(\alpha,\beta)$. Then $\alpha^2+\beta^2$ is equal to ___________.
questions.key_idea: The local minimum is at $x=-\frac{\lambda}{\sqrt3}$, and the inequality reduces to $(x+2)(x+3)<0$ since $x^2+x+2>0$.
solution: $f''(x)=-6x$ is positive at $x=-\frac\lambda{\sqrt3}$, so the point of local minimum is $x=-\frac{\lambda}{\sqrt3}$; it must satisfy $\frac{x^2+x+2}{x^2+5x+6}<0$.
$x^2+x+2>0$ for all real $x$ (discriminant $1-8<0$), so the inequality is equivalent to $\frac1{(x+2)(x+3)}<0$.
questions.correction_note: PDF replaces (x^2+x+2)/((x+2)(x+3)) by 1/((x+2)(x+3)), which is not equal; only the sign matters since x^2+x+2>0, so the interval (-3,-2) is right. The justification (x^2+x+2>0, and f''>0 at the local minimum) was added. Answer 39 unchanged.

alternate_solutions.idea: At a critical point $\lambda^2=3x^2$, so $\lambda^2$ runs over $\left(3\cdot4,\,3\cdot9\right)$ without taking square roots.
solution: $f'(x)=-3x^2+\lambda^2=0$ gives $\lambda^2=3x^2$ at the critical points; $\lambda>0$ and the minimum is at the negative one, $x=-\frac\lambda{\sqrt3}$.
Then $\lambda^2=3x^2\in(12,27)$ and, with $\lambda>0$, the interval is $(\alpha,\beta)$ with $\alpha^2=12$, $\beta^2=27$.

useful_results: For $f=-x^3+kx+c$ (negative leading coefficient) the local minimum is at the smaller critical point and the local maximum at the larger; $f''=-6x$.
Sign of a rational function: a quadratic with negative discriminant and positive leading coefficient is always positive and can be dropped from a sign analysis.
If a parameter enters only through $x^2$ at the critical points ($\lambda^2=3x^2$), work with $\lambda^2$ directly.
$x^2+5x+6=(x+2)(x+3)$: the sign is negative exactly between the roots $-3$ and $-2$.

concepts: Local extrema of an integral function (Leibniz / FTC)
Sign scheme of a product with odd and even powers
questions.question: Let $S=(-1,\infty)$ and $f:S\to\mathbb{R}$ be defined as $f(x)=\int_{-1}^{x}\left(e^t-1\right)^{11}(2t-1)^5(t-2)^7(t-3)^{12}(2t-10)^{61}dt$. Let $p=$ sum of squares of the values of $x$, where $f(x)$ attains local maxima on $S$, and $q=$ sum of the values of $x$, where $f(x)$ attains local minima on $S$. Then, the value of $p^2+2q$ is ___________.
questions.key_idea: $f'(x)$ is the integrand; only factors with an odd power change its sign, so $x=3$ (power $12$) is neither a maximum nor a minimum.
solution: By the Fundamental Theorem of Calculus, $f'(x)=\left(e^x-1\right)^{11}(2x-1)^5(x-2)^7(x-3)^{12}(2x-10)^{61}$.
The powers $11,5,7,61$ are odd, so $f'$ changes sign at $0,\frac12,2,5$; the power $12$ is even, so it does not change sign at $3$.

For $x>5$ every factor is positive, so $f'>0$. Moving left, the sign alternates at $5,\,2,\,\frac12,\,0$ (and not at $3$): $+$ on $(-1,0)$, $-$ on $\left(0,\frac12\right)$, $+$ on $\left(\frac12,2\right)$, $-$ on $(2,5)$, $+$ on $(5,\infty)$.
Local minima ($-$ to $+$) at $x=\frac12$ and $x=5$; local maxima ($+$ to $-$) at $x=0$ and $x=2$; $x=3$ gives neither.
useful_results: If $f(x)=\int_a^x\varphi(t)\,dt$ then $f'(x)=\varphi(x)$; local extrema of $f$ are the sign changes of $\varphi$.
Wavy-curve rule: a root of odd multiplicity changes the sign of $f'$, a root of even multiplicity does not (no extremum there).
Sign of the factors $\left(e^x-1\right)^{n}$: $e^x-1$ has the sign of $x$, and $2x-10$ the sign of $x-5$ - replace each factor by the simple linear factor with the same sign.
The domain $S=(-1,\infty)$ is open: an endpoint $-1$ is not a point of local extremum of $f$ on $S$.
